title: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain
summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we meet a group of youth who are helping people understand the impact of climate change on brain health; find out just how super this year's El Niño is…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it’s Bridget! When I heard there was an internship where Canadian youth were learning about how climate change and brain health are connected, while also creating accessible resources to teach others, I knew I had to find out more.

blocks.text: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain

A screenshot from a virtual showcase held on Oct. 18, where students from around the country presented the neuroscience research projects they had been working on this summer. (Brain Climate Equity Collaborative)

Doctors know that climate impacts such as wildfire smoke and extreme heat lead to physical ailments like asthma and heat exhaustion. But more research has been coming out about how climate-related events are also harming the brain, and are linked to anxiety and higher rates of dementia and cognitive functioning issues.

Neuroscience graduate student Muskaan Laroyia researches how climate change affects neurological conditions — something she has discussed at length with others in the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine.
“There was a huge gap between how we perceive brain health, and the impact that the climate crisis is having on brain health,” said Laroyia.
Laroyia co-founded the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative to empower young people to do something about it, as they are most affected by eco-anxiety.

“Recent research has said that the best way to approach eco-anxiety, especially in youth, is not just to tell them all the negative things that are happening but to help them be a part of that change,” she said.

One of the ways Laroyia and her colleagues are addressing this is through their NeuroClimate Youth Internship, launched this year with the University of Calgary’s O'Brien Institute for Public Health. The goal is to help youth learn more about the link between climate change and brain health, and then help them turn that knowledge into action.
Safina Pamery’s group worked over the summer to create accessible resources about the impacts of climate on brain health. (Submitted by Safina Pamery)

From July to October, 30 high school students from across the country worked with researchers and clinicians to explore the intersections of climate change, brain health and health equity. The students attended expert lectures, including a talk from a neuroscientist from Stanford, and a panel with the creators of the University of Toronto’s MedComic Con talking about different ways to disseminate information creatively.
By the end of the internship, the students had produced accessible digital resources for health-care professionals and the public highlighting climate impacts on the brain and what to do about them.
They created websites, presentations and short stories covering everything from how wildfire smoke and air quality affect the brain to how to recognize eco-anxiety and respond to it in healthy ways.
The internship culminated in a virtual international showcase on Oct. 18, where the students presented their research projects and answered questions from researchers, clinicians and other attendees.
Khushi Laroyia led her group’s work on extreme heat and the neurological effects it can have. (Submitted by Khushi Laroyia)

Coincidentally, Laroyia's younger sister, Khushi Laroyia, was among the students chosen by an independent committee to participate in the program. Khushi Laroyia says she learned a lot about how much climate change can impact health equity in vulnerable communities, such as older adults, people with mental health conditions, and those without access to air conditioning and cool spaces.
“Before this internship, I never thought about how climate change doesn't just affect the environment — it affects people, it affects their brain, it affects their mental health,” she said.
“It really opened my eyes to things that I wouldn't ordinarily think about.”
Her group created a website with interactive guides, case studies and toolkits with resources to help people cope with eco-anxiety and figure out how to take action.
Making information accessible

Samarth Yandhe, 15, participated in the internship from Mississauga. Yandhe interviewed people in his community to find real-life examples of how people are struggling with smoke and was surprised to learn that people were not very informed about microscopic particles called PM2.5 that can affect brain function.
He turned research and statistics into short text blurbs that anyone could understand with no prior knowledge of the science.
Samarth Yandhe, 15, is one of the youngest internship participants. He now hopes to study neuroscience at university. (Submitted by Samarth Yandhe)
“Learning about this in more detail made me think about how I spend my day,” said Yandhe, who says the project has made him think differently about things like water usage and littering.

He now realizes that all environmental degradation can harm human health, including the brain, whereas actions to improve the environment, such as conserving water and picking up trash, can improve people's health.
“If I want to help our community and others, I have to start being the type of person who would change for others.”
This is exactly what the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative is meant to inspire — a new understanding of how climate and the brain are interconnected.
“Research is very siloed, it remains in journals, and what we're trying to do is bring that information out to the public,” said Daniela Oboh, the co-executive director of the Collaborative.
There are also plans underway for another internship cohort next year, and Laroyia and Oboh have already received interest from medical schools and community organizations.
And the students haven’t stopped at the presentations. They continue to share their work through ongoing community activities, lectures and articles.
“I'm so proud of these students,” said Oboh. “Our future is very, very bright.”
— Bridget Stringer-Holden

For bat moms looking for a place to raise their pups, it’s not the rent that’s through the roof, it’s the temperature. Reader feedback

Last week, Emily Chung wrote about ways to make wind turbines less deadly to migratory bats. The article included an error: It said wind turbine curtailment happens between sunrise and sunset. In fact, it happens between sunset and sunrise. That has been corrected in the web version of the story.

Virginia Call wrote that regulations to protect bats from wind turbines are lacking in Manitoba compared to other provinces: "According to Craig Willis at U of Winnipeg, Alberta's guidelines should easily be adopted here in Manitoba. Thanks for this piece in time for Halloween, when bat-migration has just ended."

Kendyll Woodman wrote: "Thank you so much for the article on bats. I’ve loved bats since my childhood when my dad told me they eat mosquitoes. When I lived in Lesotho in Southern Africa my attic was filled with bats. Each evening around sunset I would watch as they flew away for their night time hunting. And speaking of extinction I highly recommend the novel Beasts of the Sea by Iida Turpeinen."

Gillian Arsenault and John Virag asked if vertical axis wind turbines, like some of the ones in our 2023 article on rooftop wind turbines (see animation below), might be safer for birds and bats. VAWT companies such as Freen and Wind Harvest and some researchers argue that they likely are, because the turbines spin more slowly, are more visible and cause less extreme pressure changes around them. However, Wind Harvest acknowledges that no large-scale studies have been done to verify this.
(IBIS Power/YouTube)

The Big Picture: The Super El Niño
(Climate Central)

At the beginning of the year, no one could have predicted just how strong an El Niño would develop. But by June, it became clear that not only would we be getting an El Niño, but it could be one for the record books.

In its June monthly update, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said that there was a chance that the El Niño “would rank among the largest El Niño events in the historical record going back to 1950.” And boy were they right.

Here’s what that really means: El Niño is part of a natural cycle where ocean temperatures in a particular region of the Pacific Ocean rise above average. Anything more than 2 C is considered a strong El Niño. Well, the temperature anomaly has risen to 3.5 C. That’s why some people are calling it a “super” El Niño.

As you can see above, the ocean temperature is a sweltering 30 C in the part of the central Pacific near the equator used to monitor El Niño events. And it hasn’t even peaked yet. That’s forecast to happen in either November or December. Why does this matter? It influences weather patterns around the world, with the largest impacts being droughts and heavy rainfall in regions mainly around the equator. For Canada, it means dry conditions in the already drought-stricken regions in the west and warmer temperatures across northern and central Canada. And an El Niño also helps to drive up the annual global temperature, which is already rising due to climate change.
— Nicole Mortillaro

items: The power-hungriness of AI now has companies retrofitting old jet engine turbines to provide more electricity to data centres. A solution that’s both polluting and costly.

In rural areas and colonias in Arizona, a state with a much higher maternal mortality rate than the national average, the dangers for pregnancies carried out near pesticide-sprayed fields is something state health plans don’t take into account, The Margin reports.

The gas-powered cars on Disneyland's Autopia ride have felt "stubbornly behind the times" considering the ride's location in Tomorrowland, says Rick Lye of Disney Fanatic. They're finally electrifying, but not with battery-electric technology. Lye explains what they're doing instead and why.

Some kinds of fishing are often allowed in marine protected areas. Greenpeace is trying to make that physically impossible. The group claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling” by doing this.

For more than a century, colonial policies disrupted and outlawed the practice of cultural burning in Canada, viewing fire as a threat and something to immediately suppress. Here's why Indigenous-led fire management is starting to be recognized as essential for Canada’s future, the Narwhal reports.

blocks.text: Hungry animals and local farmers want your leftover Halloween pumpkins
Justine Beaumont and her pig, Cupcake, pose alongside the pile of leftover pumpkins that people have donated to Beaumont Acres after Halloween on Nov. 2. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Some southwestern Ontario farms and municipalities are encouraging residents to keep pumpkins out of the trash as the Halloween season comes to an end.
The Great Pumpkin Rescue is an Oxford County-based volunteer group that shares ways people can repurpose their pumpkins, including through recipes, donations and composting.

“There are, quite frankly, benefits to the community when you find a locale [that's] going to take them,” said volunteer Bryan Smith. “Southwestern Ontario will grow as farmers grow more food and sell that locally, which is good for us more broadly … because it’s stimulating the local economy.”
The initiative to repurpose pumpkins started more than a decade ago at Northlane Farm in Thamesford, Ont., which to this day collects pumpkins for its farming operations.
Now, the Great Pumpkin Rescue group compiles an annual list of area farms that will take pumpkins, squash and gourds during the first week of November.
“There are quite a number of extremely happy goats, pigs and chickens who just love to eat them,” Smith said. “We want them to be turned into something that feeds farm animals.”
Hungry hogs want your Halloween leftovers

Beaumont Acres, a sanctuary in London, Ont., has been accepting pumpkins from community members every fall since it opened six years ago. Founder Justine Beaumont estimates the farm has already received close to 100 pumpkins and gourds this year.
“Our animals love pumpkins and they’re also great for them. They are great for their gut health and great for their skin,” Beaumont said.
Beaumont Acres is home to nearly 30 rescue and retired working animals, including horses, pigs, ducks and a cow.
“Our cow, Trixie, loves pumpkins. She’ll come running across the field for them,” she said.
Trixie the cow is one of the many animals at Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., that enjoys eating pumpkins. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Beaumont said each animal likes a different part of the pumpkin: horses like the seeds, ducks and chickens like the gooey insides, and pigs will eat everything.
“Our pigs also love to play with the pumpkins. They find it very stimulating. They’ll roll them around and play with them like they’re a ball,” Beaumont said. “It’s a lot of fun to watch.”
No paint, no candles allowed
It’s important to assess the condition of pumpkins before deciding where to take them, Smith said, adding that any uncarved pumpkins can be used for homemade meals.

For residents planning to take pumpkins to local animal farms, Smith said it’s important to ensure they are clean and in good condition. Pumpkins should not have any paint, metal, toothpicks, candles, wax or other unsafe-to-eat substances on — or in — them, he said.
Beaumont said it’s fine if pumpkins come to her farm a bit squishy, but she is asking people to refrain from bringing anything with mould.
At Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., Cupcake the pig enjoys a gourd and piece of pumpkin that nearby residents donated to the farm. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Better options for mouldy and broken pumpkins include sending them to farms with a digester, Smith said, which breaks down organic materials to produce energy.
Put pumpkins in municipal green bins
It's not just farmers doing the work.

Some municipalities are making it easier for residents who want to give pumpkins a second life. Both Woodstock and Tillsonburg, Ont., are offering to collect pumpkins and redistribute them to people who want them for food or livestock.
Of course, another option is always to put the pumpkins in your green bin.
However, generally, if pumpkins are painted, they must go in the garbage.
— Kendra Seguin
